items.a: Companies assumed that high-quality goods would bring success
w: Companies studied the needs of every customer
Companies reduced their prices every year
items.ref: Companies took for granted that their business would be successful if they produced high-quality goods.

items.p: Why did the model start to change?
items.a: The number of competitors grew and trade became more global
items.ref: With more competitors and an overabundance of goods, the model started to change.

items.p: What is the priority of the concept of marketing?
items.a: Customers' satisfaction
items.ref: The concept of marketing considers customers' satisfaction the priority.

items.a: A particular group of customers
items.ref: The target market is a particular group of customers chosen in the marketing strategy.

items.p: What happens in the implementation and control step?
items.a: Companies monitor results and modify the marketing mix
items.ref: After the launch, companies constantly monitor results and modify the marketing mix.

items.a: Collecting and analysing information about what people want, need and buy
w: Producing goods at a lower cost
items.ref: It is the process of collecting and analysing information about what people want, need and buy.

items.a: Research conducted directly with consumers to collect new information
items.ref: Primary research is conducted directly with consumers and collects new information (primary data).

items.p: Which is an example of field research?
items.a: A focus group
items.ref: Examples of primary research: surveys, consumer panels and focus groups.

items.p: What is a disadvantage of secondary (desk) research?
items.a: Data are not always relevant or updated
items.ref: Desk research is cheaper than field research, but data are not always relevant or updated.

items.a: Descriptive information, such as opinions and beliefs
items.ref: Qualitative data are descriptive information which cannot be measured numerically.

items.a: Segmentation, Targeting and Positioning
items.ref: STP is an acronym for Segmentation, Targeting and Positioning.

items.a: A smaller group of the market with similar characteristics
items.ref: In segmentation the market is divided into smaller groups with similar characteristics.

items.a: Geographic
items.ref: Geographic (where?), demographic (who?), psychographic (why?), behavioural (how?).

items.a: Evaluating each segment and selecting the most attractive ones
items.ref: Targeting is the evaluation of the commercial attractiveness of each segment and the selection of the target market.

items.p: What does a market map show?
items.a: The positions a product can take according to price and quality
items.ref: A market map shows the positions a product can take on the market according to price and quality.

items.a: Product, price, promotion, place
items.ref: The 4Ps are product, price, promotion and place.

items.a: Features that make a product different, like design or colour
w: The lowest prices on the market
items.ref: Manufacturers differentiate products through features that become their Unique Selling Points.

items.p: Which two kinds of factors influence the price?
items.a: Internal and external factors
items.ref: Price is set by considering internal factors (production cost) and external factors (competing prices).

items.p: What does 'promotion' mean in the marketing mix?
items.a: How customers are informed about products
items.ref: Promotion is the process of making a business and its products known to potential customers.

items.p: Which are the three extra Ps of the 7Ps?
items.a: Physical evidence, process and people
items.ref: The extended marketing mix adds physical evidence, process and people.

items.a: A technique to differentiate products from competitors' ones
w: A way to reduce production costs
items.ref: Branding is a technique used by companies to differentiate their products from competitors' ones.

items.p: Which is an example of a brand name that is an invented word?
items.a: Google
items.ref: Invented words: Google. Family names: McDonald's. Descriptive: General Motors. Geographical: American Airlines.

items.a: Products that supermarkets market under their own name
items.ref: Supermarket chains buy products from manufacturers and market them under their name or a new brand name.

items.a: A low price to enter a new market and gain market share
w: A very high price for exclusivity
A price just below a round number
A price reduced for one year
items.ref: Penetration price: offering a low price to enter a new market and/or gain market share.

items.a: A price just below a round number, like 9,99
w: A price much higher than competitors
A price fixed by the government
items.ref: Odd or psychological prices create the perception of a good deal (9,99 instead of 10).

items.p: Why do companies need digital marketing strategies?
items.a: To reach target customers on the platforms they use most
w: To reduce the number of customers
items.ref: Companies need to reach their target customers on the platforms they use the most.

items.a: Online material that sparks interest without directly promoting a brand
items.ref: Content marketing creates online material that doesn't directly promote a brand but sparks interest in its products.

items.a: Search Engine Optimisation
items.ref: Search Engine Optimisation: most customers use searches to find products and services.

items.p: Which is a challenge of digital marketing?
items.a: Complying with privacy and data sharing regulations
items.ref: Companies need to comply with privacy laws, some of them transnational (GDPR).

items.a: Using email, social media, website, SEO and newsletters together
items.ref: Omnichannel strategies include email, social media, website, SEO and newsletters.
